mainEntity.name: How much does a cedar privacy fence cost in Clarkston, Michigan?

acceptedAnswer.text: A cedar privacy fence in the Clarkston area generally runs $35-$40 per linear foot installed in 2026, with high-grade western red cedar higher, from $45 to $90 per linear foot. A typical 200-linear-foot cedar project runs $3,700 to $9,300, averaging around $6,500. Wooded acreage lots usually need longer runs and include a terrain adjustment — a moderate slope typically adds about 25% in labor, and a steep stepped run up to 50% — so expect a 300-foot-plus run plus a driveway gate to land above the typical 200-foot benchmark. Get a written, itemized estimate for your specific lot.

mainEntity.name: Do I need a permit for a fence in the Village of Clarkston or Independence Township?

acceptedAnswer.text: Your zoning rules depend on which of the two you live in — the Village of Clarkston has its own zoning ordinance, and Independence Township has a separate one — but permitting for both is administered through the Independence Township Building Department at 6483 Waldon Center Drive (248-625-8111, Monday-Thursday, 7:00 a.m.-5:30 p.m.). Michigan Residential Code generally exempts standard residential fences under 7 feet from building permit requirements, but local zoning still governs height, placement, and materials, and the township's ordinance regulates fences under Article 10, Section 10.05. Confirm your district (R-1A through R-1R) and any deed restrictions before you dig.

mainEntity.name: How deep should fence posts be set in Michigan?

acceptedAnswer.text: Michigan Residential Code R403.1.4 requires exterior footings to extend 42 inches below grade, and Michigan frost depth runs 42 to 48 inches depending on the region. Best practice is to set the bottom of the footing at least 6 inches below the published frost line, so a 6-foot privacy fence commonly uses an 8-foot post with 48 inches in the ground. The old one-third-of-the-post-in-the-ground rule gives you about 36 inches on a 6-foot fence, which is not deep enough in Michigan clay. Gate and corner posts should go 4 to 6 inches deeper than line posts.

mainEntity.name: What is the best fence material for a wooded lot in Michigan?

acceptedAnswer.text: For the visible parts of the fence, western red cedar is the best balance of longevity, appearance, and Michigan weather performance; it weathers to silver-gray or takes a stain well and holds up through freeze-thaw cycles. For the posts, pressure-treated lumber is the right choice because it's the part in permanent ground contact. Vinyl and composite are legitimate alternatives, especially in newer subdivisions with strict CC&Rs, and both will cost more up front. The hybrid spec — cedar pickets and rails on pressure-treated posts — is what most Michigan homeowners end up choosing.

mainEntity.name: Can you install a fence around trees without killing them?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually, yes, if the fence line is planned before any digging happens. Roots inside the fence trench get cut by hand, cleanly, rather than being torn out with a machine. Where a large tree sits directly in the line, the better approach is to jog the fence around the trunk and build a short return, which gives the tree root space and keeps the run looking intentional. Fencing right up against a large trunk is the pattern that causes decline, because the root flare stays wet and the trunk can't breathe.

mainEntity.name: What does a double driveway gate cost in Michigan?

acceptedAnswer.text: In 2026, a simple 10-foot driveway gate runs around $800, a basic double gate typically adds $300 to $1,000 or more to a fence project, and a double driveway gate with automated openers generally runs $1,200 to $3,500 or more depending on width, hardware, and whether a power run is needed. Gate posts have to be sized up and set 4 to 6 inches deeper than line posts, and each swinging leaf needs diagonal bracing, so gates should be planned at the start of the project rather than added to a finished fence line.

mainEntity.name: How long does a fence installation take on an acreage lot?

acceptedAnswer.text: A typical suburban yard can be fenced in a few days, but a long run on a wooded acreage lot takes longer — plan on a working week or more for roughly 340 feet with grade changes, tree conflicts, and two gates, since footings need time to cure before load goes on them. Material staging and access on a long run add time as well. The other timeline is booking: fall is the best install window in Michigan and September is typically booked 1 to 3 weeks out.

mainEntity.name: Will a fence keep deer out of my garden in Clarkston?

acceptedAnswer.text: A 6-foot fence changes deer movement and protects most of what's behind it, but a determined deer on a hard winter can still get through or over a standard residential fence, and Independence Township does carry heavy deer pressure given the habitat around Independence Oaks County Park. The realistic approach is a 6-foot cedar privacy fence as the perimeter, plus protection for young or especially palatable plantings inside it for their first few winters. Anyone promising that a 6-foot wood fence eliminates deer browsing is overstating what any fence can do.
